item_name: Learning to Track - Online MOT by Decision Making (Xiang, Alahi, Savarese, ICCV 2015) and deep RL association/decision trackers (Ren et al. ECCV 2018; Rosello & Kochenderfer AAMAS 2018)
bibliography: [S1] Yu Xiang, Alexandre Alahi, Silvio Savarese. Learning to Track: Online Multi-Object Tracking by Decision Making. ICCV 2015, pp. 4705-4713. PDF: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_iccv_2015/papers/Xiang_Learning_to_Track_ICCV_2015_paper.pdf . Official code (MATLAB, MIT licence): https://github.com/yuxng/MDP_Tracking (repository verified to exist via GitHub API; files MDP_train.m, MDP_reward_occluded.m, MDP_value.m, globals.m opened). [S2] Liangliang Ren, Jiwen Lu, Zifeng Wang, Qi Tian, Jie Zhou (Tsinghua University; Qi Tian then UTSA). Collaborative Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Object Tracking (C-DRL). ECCV 2018, LNCS, pp. 586-602, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-01219-9_36. PDF: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ECCV_2018/papers/Liangliang_Ren_Collaborative_Deep_Reinforcement_ECCV_2018_paper.pdf . No official code link in the paper; no official repository found in this short check [uncertain]. [S3] Pol Rosello, Mykel J. Kochenderfer (Stanford). Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Object Tracking (MARLMOT). AAMAS 2018 (full paper, 8 pages, Session 37), pp. 1397-1404. PDF: https://ifmas.csc.liv.ac.uk/Proceedings/aamas2018/pdfs/p1397.pdf . No code link in the paper. Independence: the three are independent groups and systems; S2 cites S1 as a prior Markov-decision online tracker; S3 compares only to SORT and RNN baselines and mentions S1 in passing. No preprint/journal duplicates were used.
full_text_checked: S1: full main text (9 pages, PDF text extraction) including Algorithm 1 and 2, Tables 1-4; Figure 4 (component ablation bar chart) and Figure 5 values only partly legible in text extraction - Figure 4 bar heights not read numerically. Code files read: MDP_train.m (training loop, lines ~41-300), MDP_reward_occluded.m (lost-state reward/label rule, full), MDP_value.m (test-time lost-state decision, grep of key lines), globals.m (thresholds, grep), MDP_test.m (grep only). No supplementary/technical report opened. S2: full main text (17 pages incl. references) via PDF text extraction: Sections 3-5, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-4, Fig. 4 caption. No supplementary, no code. S3: full main text (8 pages) via PDF text extraction: Sections 3-5, Table 1 (action space), Table 2, Fig. 4 caption; simulated scenario section read only partially.
inputs_state_output: S1 (MDP tracker): inputs = public ACF detections + RGB frames; per-target MDP with state subspaces Active/Tracked/Lost/Inactive; internal memory = K stored image templates of the target from tracked frames (K=10 at test; Table 3 explores 1-12) plus a 'lazy' tracking template and a linear motion model; Tracked-state uses Lucas-Kanade optical flow with forward-backward error and mean overlap with detections over the last frames. Lost-state output = a score f(t,d)=w'phi(t,d)+b for every (lost target, detection not covered by a tracked target) pair, phi is a 12-d hand-crafted similarity vector (FB errors on 5 template parts, two NCC terms, two height ratios, flow-predicted-box overlap, detection score, centre distance after linear motion prediction; Table 1); scores feed a Hungarian assignment among lost targets. Code additionally hard-gates candidates (aspect ratio threshold 0.6, distance <= 3 target widths) before the classifier. S2 (C-DRL): input = 107x107 RGB crops; prediction network (MDNet-like conv features 512-d + 10-frame box history) regresses next-frame box shift (trained to maximise IoU); decision network input 2060-d = features of the agent prediction, its nearest neighbouring agent, its nearest detection in the next frame, and the agent's previous-frame feature; output = 4 action logits. Appearance memory = exponential moving average of features. S3 (MARLMOT): vision-free; each agent owns a Kalman filter; 18-d observation = prior prediction (7), associated detection box (4), detection confidence, Hungarian association cost, one-hot track mode (3), frames since last association, consecutive-association streak; shared 3-layer MLP (128-64-32) -> softmax over 5 actions. Comparison with ours: our readout is closest to S3 in spirit (a small per-candidate head that sees geometry plus assignment-context features: own cost, competing costs, margin, assigned flag) and to S1 in structure (per-candidate score over real detections with an implicit 'stay' option), but ours adds 68 FlyVis regional activity features per real region from a recurrent state that ran over exemplar and search frames, and an observed-target descriptor. None of the three sources uses a recurrent sensory state comparable to FlyVis; S1's 'history' is a bank of raw templates, S2's is a 10-frame box history plus EMA feature, S3's is two counters. None scores multiple candidate regions inside a bounded eye: S1 scores all uncovered detections (whole frame, gated), S2 looks at only one nearest detection and one nearest neighbour, S3 only at the one detection the Hungarian solver already associated.
action_and_refusal: S1: actions are state transitions; in Lost state the choice is 'link to detection d_k' (a6, transfer to Tracked; the tracking template is replaced by the detection box) versus 'stay lost' (a5); abstention is the sign of the max-margin score (y=-1 if f<0 for all candidates; in code the SVM probability/label via svmpredict -b 1), so refusal is a learned classification boundary, not a tuned threshold on a regression output. Lost > T_lost (code max_occlusion=50) -> Inactive. Tracked targets have priority and their detections are suppressed before lost-target association. S2: per-agent action set {update (fuse prediction and detection, update EMA appearance), ignore (use prediction only), block (keep feature, propagate by prediction - occlusion), delete}; unmatched detections spawn agents, false agents are expected to choose delete. S3: Table 1 actions a1 terminate, a2 restart the filter from the associated detection (state and covariance replaced by the detection box), a3 normal Kalman update, a4 ignore the detection and propagate (explicit refusal of the associated detection), a5 propagate into hidden mode. Comparison: our full-box transfer of a selected real region into the track state is directly analogous to S3 a2 and to S1's lost->tracked relink with template replacement; our fixed logit 0 'no action' corresponds to S1 'stay lost' / S3 a4. Difference: in S1 and S3 the default/refusal is one of the classes the policy is trained to predict with real labels; in our head the no-action option is a constant logit not trained against, so the decision boundary depends on the absolute scale of regressed scores.
labels_and_loss: S1 (key for this item): the Lost-state classifier is trained by an on-policy mistake-driven loop (Algorithm 1; the paper calls it reinforcement learning, but it is closer to DAgger-style imitation of a ground-truth expert). For every training target the current policy tracks it from its first correctly detected frame; only when, in a Lost state, the policy's action differs from the action implied by ground truth is one example added: (i) wrong association -> phi(t,d_k) labelled negative; (ii) missed association while the target is visible and correctly detected -> positive. The SVM is retrained on the growing set and the episode for that target ends ('game over' in MDP_reward_occluded.m) and is restarted later; training stops when all targets are tracked successfully. Neutral situations give reward 0 and produce no example (code: reward 0 when no GT-overlapping detection and tracker overlap between overlap_neg=0.2 and overlap_pos=0.5, or when the target is still flagged as just-lost); correct non-association during occlusion (GT covered > 0.7) gives reward +1 and no example. Rare/hard events: handled implicitly by only collecting mistakes encountered under the current policy (hard-example mining): 1,397 examples versus 45,005 for the offline variant (Section 4.2); targets that still fail after max_count=10 attempts are marked 'difficult' and skipped (code, globals.m max_count=10, max_pass=2, max_iter=10000). Loss: soft-margin SVM (Eq. 4; paper says linear, released code calls libsvm with '-g 1 -b 1', i.e. default RBF kernel with probability outputs - a paper/code discrepancy). Labels are immediate ground-truth correctness of the (target, detection) pair (IoU > 0.5 with the GT box), not downstream tracking metric consequences. Active-state SVM is trained offline on detection-vs-GT labels; Tracked-state rule uses hand thresholds. S2: reward per agent r_i,t in {+1 if IoU>=0.7, 0 if 0.5<=IoU<=0.7, -1 otherwise} for update/ignore/block (IoU of the resulting location with next-frame GT), delete gets +1 if the object disappeared else -1; spawned false detections get -1 for non-delete actions; collaborative reward r* = r_i,t + beta*r_j,t+1 of the nearest neighbour (beta=0.4), discounted return with gamma=0.8 (grid-searched on MOT15 train, Fig. 4). Loss: REINFORCE with an advantage A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s), V(s)=sum_a p(a|s)Q(s,a) (Eqs. 12-14); the authors state the plain Q-weighted gradient did not converge because Q values were all positive in easy scenes and all negative in hard ones - a direct parallel to our good-minus-harm scale problem. How Q for untaken actions is obtained for Eq. 12 is not specified [uncertain]. No explicit class rebalancing. S3: per-frame joint reward r_t = -(misses + false positives + mismatches)_t / sum_t g_t so that the undiscounted episode return equals the sequence MOTA (Eq. 6-7); TRPO (rllab), lr 1e-4, gamma 0.95, no value baseline; observation normalisation and 'representative batches' (one rollout per training sequence per batch) were required to beat SORT (Fig. 4). Rarity is not treated explicitly; the metric-level return dilutes per-decision credit.
data_camera_resolution_rate: S1: 2D MOT 2015 benchmark, pedestrians, public ACF detections; 11 training and 11 test sequences; validation analysis uses 5 training sequences (TUD-Stadtmitte, ETH-Bahnhof, ADL-Rundle-6, KITTI-13, PETS09-S2L1) and 6 validation test sequences (TUD-Campus, ETH-Sunnyday, ETH-Pedcross2, ADL-Rundle-8, Venice-2, KITTI-17), Table 2; for the official test one classifier is trained per scenario-matched training sequence group (6 similarity functions). Mixed static and moving cameras (ETH, KITTI moving platforms), resolutions from 640x480 to 1920x1080, frame rates from 2.5 fps (AVG-TownCentre) to 30 fps; initial condition: targets start from detections passing the Active SVM. S2: MOT15 (11/11) and MOT16 (7/7) public detections; the decision network was trained on all training sequences of MOT15 and MOT16 for 10 epochs; ablations run on MOT15 training set with SubCNN detections (i.e. on training data); crops 107x107. S3: one simulated scenario plus MOT15 training set (11 sequences) with public detections; 'Train on all' trained and evaluated on the same 11 training sequences; 'Train on 1' trained on 1 sequence and evaluated on all 11 (includes the training one). No input image resolution (vision-free). Compared with our setup (BDD100K MOT, YOLO26s detections, vehicles and pedestrians, moving vehicle camera, bounded grey FlyVis eye crop, train26/fit20 split with paired bootstrap over videos), all three use far fewer independent videos and no confidence intervals.
metrics_and_numbers: Authors' CLEAR-MOT metrics only; not translatable into HOTA for our bench. S1 Table 4 (MOT15 test): MDP REL (on-policy RL) MOTA 30.3, MOTP 71.3, MT 13.0%, ML 38.4%, FP 9,717, FN 32,422, IDS 680, Frag 1,500, 1.1 Hz; MDP OFL (same features and framework, classifier trained offline on 45,005 GT-linked pairs) MOTA 30.1, MOTP 71.6, MT 10.4%, ML 41.3%, FP 8,789, FN 33,479, IDS 690, Frag 1,301; best other published tracker MotiCon MOTA 23.1. Table 3 (validation, number of templates K): MOTA ranges 19.5 (K=6) to 26.7 (K=5 and K=9), non-monotonic. Section 4.2: REL used 1,397 training examples vs 45,005 for OFL (about 3%). S2 Table 3 (MOT15 test): MOTA 37.1, MOTP 71.0, MT 14.0%, ML 31.3%, FP 7,036, FN 30,440 (MDP [S1] listed at 30.3); Table 4 (MOT16 test): MOTA 47.3, MOTP 74.6, MT 17.4%, ML 39.9%, FP 6,375, FN 88,543. Table 2 (ablation, MOT15 training set, SubCNN detections): full model MOTA 67.8, IDs 307, FP 4,995; decision network replaced by Hungarian MOTA 54.9, IDs 2,048, FP 9,042; prediction network replaced by velocity model MOTA 63.3, IDs 453; MDNet features replaced by colour histogram MOTA 65.9, IDs 463. Table 1: inter-frame threshold 1-9 gives MOTA 63-67. S3 Table 2 (MOT15 training set, public detections): MARLMOT train-on-all MOTA 27.7, MOTP 72.5, FP 6,092, FN 21,976, IDs 767, MT 75, ML 236; train-on-1 MOTA 24.0, IDs 784; SORT-Public MOTA 26.0, IDs 780, FP 6,767, FN 21,988; RNN-LSTM 22.3.
distinguishing_ablations: S1: the only test isolating 'learning from decision consequences' is MDP REL vs MDP OFL on the MOT15 test set (Table 4): MOTA 30.3 vs 30.1, IDS 680 vs 690 - a single submission each, no seeds, no interval; the difference is within noise, so the paper supports sample efficiency (3% of the examples) and on-policy hard-example mining, not a recovery-quality gain. Figure 4 (validation, MOTA when disabling components): disabling lost-state association a6 causes a large drop and more than 3x ID switches; disabling template tracking a3 has little effect; disabling FB-error, NCC, height-ratio or distance features each reduces MOTA, distance the most; overlap and detection score have no effect (bar heights not read numerically). Table 3 shows strong non-monotonic sensitivity to the number of templates (19.5-26.7 MOTA), indicating high variance on 6 sequences. Fig. 5 cross-domain train/test pairs show scenario dependence. Mandatory components for the claim: the lost-state association decision itself; the on-policy loop matters for efficiency only. S2: Table 2 replaces the decision network by Hungarian (MOTA 67.8 -> 54.9, IDs 307 -> 2,048), but this is evaluated on MOT15 training sequences that were part of the decision network's training data, a single run, and the Hungarian baseline is not tuned - it does not isolate RL vs supervised learning of the same decision, nor the collaborative reward term (beta is only grid-searched on training reward, Fig. 4, no tracking-metric ablation of beta=0). Authors' limitations (Section 4.6 discussion): agents lost for more than 2 frames are deleted, causing ID switches at high frame rate; similar position/appearance of crossing objects causes switches. S3: Fig. 4 shows that observation normalisation and representative batches were needed to exceed SORT; 'train on 1' (24.0) is below SORT (26.0); all numbers are on training data; single run; authors report more FP and fragmentation and attribute fragmentation to the stochastic policy; action a5 (hidden) is never used in the simulation. Across sources: no seeds, no CIs, and no ablation that compares consequence-based training against similarity/IoU-supervised training of the identical decision head on held-out data except S1's REL vs OFL (null difference).
explanations_addressed: Lost discriminative/spatial information in readout: not addressed by any source (all use hand features or global CNN crops; S1's feature ablation shows appearance-consistency features matter, which is only a design analogy that richer target-vs-candidate comparison features help). Target-vs-neighbour identification: design analogy - S2 feeds the nearest neighbouring agent's crop into the decision network and adds the neighbour's reward to the agent's reward; S1 suppresses detections covered by tracked targets before relinking; S3 includes the association cost. None isolates this effect on held-out data. Training objective mismatched to the final assignment: direct but weak evidence - S3 optimises a return equal to MOTA and beats SORT on training data (27.7 vs 26.0); S1 shows that on-policy mistake-driven training matches offline supervised training (30.3 vs 30.1) with 3% of the data, i.e. objective alignment did not by itself improve the metric; S2 reports that a plain Q-weighted policy gradient does not converge and needs an advantage baseline (design analogy for our good-minus-harm targets whose sign/scale differs between easy and hard rows). Rare useful events with high harm cost: design analogy - S1 never trains on neutral rows (reward 0 -> no example), adds an example only when the current policy errs, ends the episode at the first harmful decision, and gives up on targets after 10 failed attempts; this is the clearest published recipe for keeping rare corrective events from being swamped by neutral ones, but its effect on the tracking metric is not demonstrated. S2's zero-reward band (IoU 0.5-0.7) is a neutral class. Insufficient history: direct evidence in S1 Table 3 (template count 1-12 changes MOTA 19.5-26.7, non-monotonic) and S2 Table 1 (inter-frame threshold); caution: large variance on small sets. Limits of the action: S3 Table 1 shows that restarting a track from the associated detection box (a2) is a useful learned action alongside ignore/propagate, analogous to our full-box transfer; S2 limitation that deletion after 2 lost frames causes switches is a caution about action horizon. Not addressed: the case where the correct detection lies outside a bounded sensory window (our 334 cases).
evidence_strength: S1: peer-reviewed ICCV 2015, official code verified (MATLAB), widely reused as a baseline; but the specific claim relevant here (consequence/on-policy learning improves recovery) rests on one test submission with a 0.2 MOTA difference and no interval - weak for that claim, moderate for the sample-efficiency claim. S2: peer-reviewed ECCV 2018, no code found [uncertain], key ablation on training data - weak. S3: peer-reviewed AAMAS 2018 full paper, no code, evaluated on its own training set, single run - weak. Overall: weak evidence that learning from decision consequences, as opposed to similarity/IoU supervision, improves recovery; moderate evidence that mistake-driven on-policy sampling is data-efficient. No independent replications of the RL-vs-supervised comparison were found in this short check.
difference_from_tried: Our latest head (z13_box_supervision_followup_v1) regresses each action score with MSE to an off-policy good-minus-harm target in {-1,0,+1} over all rows (mostly 0), then applies softmax against a fixed baseline logit 0 with a threshold tuned on 20 videos. This is closest to S1's offline variant (MDP OFL) and to a value-regression version of S2 without the advantage baseline. Genuine differences in the sources: (1) S1 trains a max-margin classifier only on decision-relevant rows (policy mistakes: harmful fires as negatives, missed helpful actions as positives), never on neutral rows - our MSE target spends most capacity predicting 0 for the 1000-3500 neutral selections, consistent with the observed probabilities never exceeding about 0.6; (2) S1 collects examples on-policy, i.e. under the track states produced by the current policy, whereas our rows come from baseline trajectories, so after a box transfer the later eye crops, FlyVis states and assignment contexts are unseen (covariate shift); (3) S1's refusal is a trained class boundary, ours a constant logit; (4) S2 uses an advantage relative to the policy-weighted mean of action values in the same state, which is a per-query centring we did not apply; (5) S3 optimises a metric-equal return. Not different: the action space (S3 a2 restart-from-detection is our full-box transfer), assignment-context features (S3 uses association cost; we already use cost, competitor cost, margin), and the use of ground-truth correctness as label (S1 labels are immediate GT IoU correctness, the same information as our fixable/harm labels). The earlier KeepTrack-style 3-peak association and category replacement are unrelated to these sources.
candidate_node_change: Node: FlyVis readout loss and sampling (readout node of the modernized fly; the FlyVis core, eye input and 68 regional features stay unchanged in the first stage). Change: replace per-action MSE regression over all rows with a mistake-driven max-margin decision loss in the style of S1: positives = real regions whose full-box transfer changes a wrong baseline outcome to correct; negatives = regions whose transfer would harm a correct outcome and regions the current head selects that are harmful; neutral rows (outcome unchanged) excluded or given a small weight; the no-action option trained as an explicit class (or a pairwise hinge 'helpful region score > no-action score > harmful region score') rather than a constant logit 0; optionally per-query advantage centring as in S2. Why it addresses a FlyVis-path problem: the readout of the fly currently fails to separate the 13-33 outcome-changing actions from thousands of neutral ones; this tests whether the failure is the training objective (fixable at the readout/loss node) or the information content of the FlyVis regional features (then the loss change will not help and the readout/representation node must change). Equal controls (same loss, same rows, same split): old D features; stock FlyVis C features; eye input R1 (pixels of the same crop without FlyVis); no-fly geometry plus assignment-context only. Fly result only if D (or the new version) beats the no-fly geometry control. Cheap distinguishing check (CPU, saved fit20/train26 calibration rows and saved features, no new FlyVis maps): fit the max-margin head by leave-videos-out over the existing split and report, on held-out videos, (a) precision of selected actions among outcome-changing rows versus the current MSE head at matched selection counts, (b) the fraction of the oracle reserve (+5.24 pp in-eye full boxes, +2.07 pp restricted to queries with supported history) captured by the decision rule, with paired bootstrap; if all four feature sets (D, C, R1, geometry) give the same ranking quality, the bottleneck is not the loss. Second stage (S1 on-policy aggregation, 2-3 rounds): rerun the bench with the current head on training videos, add only the new mistakes, retrain - requires recomputing eye crops and FlyVis states after box transfers, hence GPU. Condition to proceed to GPU/HOTA: on held-out saved rows the new loss with D features must capture a clearly positive share of the oracle reserve with a positive lower bound and exceed the no-fly geometry control; otherwise record a negative result for the loss node and move to the representation/readout node (spatial correlation instead of region pooling). The pre-registered project criterion for HOTA (+2 pp) is unchanged and not implied by these sources.
strongest_objection: The only controlled comparison in these sources between learning from decision consequences and conventional supervised learning of the same decision (S1, MDP REL vs MDP OFL) shows no metric gain (MOTA 30.3 vs 30.1, single run); S2 and S3 report gains only on training data and against weak or untuned baselines. Moreover S1's 'consequence' labels are immediate ground-truth correctness of a pair - the same information our good-minus-harm labels already contain - so the transferable part is the sampling/loss recipe (ignore neutrals, on-policy hard mistakes, trained refusal), not a new signal. Our diagnostics (only 13-33 of 1000-3500 selected actions change the outcome; probabilities never above about 0.6) are equally consistent with insufficient discriminative information in 68 region-pooled FlyVis features, which none of these sources addresses; a loss change cannot create information that the readout input lacks. Finally, RL in the full sense (S2/S3) with only ~26 training videos and rare positive events would have very high gradient variance, and S3 needed metric-level returns that dilute per-decision credit.
cost_and_hardware: Stage 1 (max-margin/mistake-driven loss on saved features and saved calibration rows, four equal feature controls, leave-videos-out, paired bootstrap): CPU only, small linear/MLP heads, roughly hours of compute [uncertain]. Stage 2 (on-policy aggregation in the style of S1, 2-3 rounds): needs new eye crops and FlyVis states after each box transfer on training videos, i.e. new FlyVis maps on the single 12 GB GPU per round; the cost scales with the number of queries re-rendered and is not estimated here [uncertain]. Full RL as in S2/S3 (policy gradient/TRPO with rollouts through the bench) is not proportionate for one GPU and ~26 training videos and is not recommended.
ranking_note: Ranks below the first-group full analyses (dense spatial correlation / Siamese box, object permanence memory) because it offers no fix for the information content of the FlyVis readout or for targets outside the eye; ranks as a cheap, CPU-testable loss/sampling-node candidate that can discriminate 'objective mismatch' from 'missing information' before any GPU work.
